Remarks

Remark 2 (Why isoperimetry does not shortcut ingredient (i)). It is tempting to replace Proposition 1(i) by a Harper/Erdős–Littlewood–Offord crowding argument, as in the distinctsubset-sums problem [1, 5], where a vertex-isoperimetric bound forces many signed sums into a short interval and pigeonhole extracts a close pair. That route is structurally unavailable here: the close pairs it produces differ in a single coordinate (Hamming distance 1), whereas the pairs counted by N (k, j) are disjoint (Hamming distance 2j). Isoperimetry crowds Hammingadjacent points; the present count needs crowding among Hamming-opposite points, and no slicing reconciles the two. The shared content with that literature is the small-ball density toolkit (Proposition 1), not the combinatorial mechanism. Remark 3 (Constants and the role of φ). A and cβ are not optimized; the robust output is  the exponent, which depends only on the shape N (k, j) ≍ k−j j , not on the O(1) prefactors. In the larger program φ is a floor rather than the growth rate: finite-k maxima exceed the φ k lower bound by bounded factors, consistent with gsf (k) ≍ φ k but not establishing a larger base, so whether the true rate equals φ or exceeds it is left open, between φ and the unconditional upper bound gsf (k) ≤ (1.88988 . . .)k proved in the companion note [4].
